title: Open-System Probe Selection and Optimal Measurements for Dispersive Coupling Metrology
authors: Achal Vinod, Da-Wei Luo, Ting Yu
abstract: We investigate how photon loss and environmental memory affect probe selection and measurement sensitivity for estimating the dispersive coupling strength in a cavity qubit system. Using density operator and quantum state diffusion approaches, we examine the quantum Fisher information for representative separable and entangled initial states in Markovian and non Markovian regimes. The results show that closed system generator variance alone does not determine open system performance. The survival of parameter sensitive coherences and the influence of environmental memory also play important roles. Within the single photon preparations examined, a separable probe can outperform the entangled family considered. Comparisons of selected coherent and squeezed vacuum preparations at equal mean photon number further illustrate how photon number statistics and qubit preparation affect sensitivity. For the parameters studied, finite environmental memory can enhance and prolong sensitivity and yield nonzero QFI for a probe whose Markovian QFI vanishes. We also numerically identify a fixed Hermitian observable whose error propagation uncertainty remains close to the quantum Cramer Rao bound over a prescribed coupling interval in the Markovian regime. These findings clarify the interplay between probe preparation, environmental dynamics, and measurement choice in dispersive quantum metrology.
summary: This paper rigorously analyzes quantum metrology in open cavity-qubit systems to estimate the coupling strength $\chi$. It demonstrates that environmental memory effects are critical, capable of boosting sensitivity beyond what is predicted by the simpler Markovian model. The findings guide the selection of optimal quantum probes and measurement protocols for noisy quantum devices.
main_problem: The paper investigates how photon loss and environmental memory affect the optimal selection of quantum probes and measurement strategies for estimating the dispersive coupling strength in a cavity-qubit system.
main_result: Finite environmental memory can significantly enhance and prolong the metrological sensitivity, allowing for non-zero Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) even when the Markovian QFI vanishes. Furthermore, separable probes can outperform entangled ones in certain single-photon regimes.
method: The analysis employs quantum metrology tools, primarily calculating the Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) using both density-operator and stochastic (trajectory-based) approaches, comparing Markovian and non-Markovian dynamics.
model_or_system: The system is a single bosonic cavity mode dispersively coupled to a two-level qubit, governed by an effective Hamiltonian. The dynamics are analyzed under open-system conditions, ranging from Markovian (Lindblad) to non-Markovian (exponentially correlated bath).
key_observables: Quantum Fisher Information (QFI), Stochastic QFI (SQFI), and the error propagation uncertainty relative to the Quantum Cramér-Rao Bound (QCRB).
important_parameters: Dispersive coupling strength ($\chi$), environmental correlation time ($	au_B$), cavity-qubit detuning ($\Delta$), and mean photon number ($\langle \hat{N} angle$).
main_assumptions: The closed-system analysis provides a benchmark, and the non-Markovian dynamics are modeled using an exponentially correlated Gaussian environment.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the time evolution of QFI for different initial states and regimes, showing the comparison between density-matrix QFI and ensemble-averaged SQFI, and mapping out parameter regions where sensitivity is enhanced.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the closed-system benchmark using the generator variance. It then transitions to open systems, comparing Markovian and non-Markovian dynamics using QFI diagnostics. The core of the work involves analyzing how environmental memory and probe preparation affect the achievable precision bound.
why_interesting: This work provides a detailed theoretical framework for designing quantum sensors in realistic, noisy environments, which is crucial for advancing quantum networking and quantum computation applications utilizing cavity QED systems.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: Time evolution of the unconditional density- matrix QFI (blue solid curve) and the ensemble-averaged SQFI obtained from QSD simulations with Ntraj = 2000 trajectories (red dashed curve). The density-matrix result is obtained by solving the Markovian Lindblad master equation, and the trajectory simulations use an integration time step ∆t = 0.01. Both curves correspond to the initial state |+, +⟩, with ωc = ωq = 1, Γ = 1, and χ = 0.2.

FIG. 2: Maximum magnitude of the non-Markovian response functions X+(t) and X−(t) over the evolution interval as a function of Ω/Γ, for ωc/Γ = 1, γ/Γ = 0.6, and χ/Γ = 0.2. The X−branch exhibits a sharp pole-like enhancement near Ω/Γ ≃0.8, while X+ remains bounded over the displayed range. The dashed vertical line marks the working point Ω/Γ = 0.2 used in the subsequent numerical calculations.

FIG. 3: Open-system QFI for representative probes. Panel (a) shows the QFI evolution for |1, +⟩(blue), |+, +⟩ (orange), and the entangled state |ψ(7π/20)⟩= cos(7π/20) |0, e⟩+sin(7π/20) |1, g⟩(green), using ωc/Γ = ωq/Γ = 1, γ/Γ = 0.6, Ω/Γ = 0.2, and χ/Γ = 0.2. Solid curves denote non-Markovian evolution and dashed curves denote Markovian evolution. Panel (b) shows the corresponding evolution for the shorter-memory case γ/Γ = 10, with all other parameters unchanged. As γ increases, the non-Markovian curves approach their Markovian counterparts, consistent with the short-memory limit derived in Sec. II C.

FIG. 4: QFI for the family |ψ(θ)⟩= cos θ |0, e⟩+sin θ |1, g⟩as a function of θ and evolution time t, for (a) Markovian and (b) non-Markovian dynamics. The reference parameters are ωc/Γ = ωq/Γ = 1, χ/Γ = 0.2, and, in panel (b), γ/Γ = 0.6 and Ω/Γ = 0.2. Both panels span 0 ≤θ ≤π and 0 ≤t ≤50. Markovian sensitivity is concentrated at early times, whereas finite memory substantially extends its persistence. The high-QFI regions lie away from the maximally entangled states at θ = π/4 and 3π/4. Color represents Fχ, with a separate numerical color scale for each panel.

FIG. 5: Non-Markovian QFI for the initial state |1, g⟩ as a function of inverse bath memory time γ and evo- lution time t; color represents Fχ. Although the closed and Markovian evolutions of this state yield zero QFI, finite environmental memory can activate sensitivity to χ. The scan exhibits appreciable sensitivity and tempo- ral structure for smaller γ, with suppression toward the short-memory side of the displayed range. No monotonic dependence on γ is implied.
